deck-5-4x6.note: Actual 1 in. x 5-1/2 in. (25 x 140 mm) as 5/4x6 decking is usually sold; the 16 in. joist spacing limit is a rule of thumb.

osb-12.name: OSB 15/32 in (nominal 1/2 in, 11.9 mm)
osb-12.note: 4 x 8 ft is exact. The thickness is the usual 15/32 in panel; not read from a panel standard. Key kept as osb-12 so a spec works in both regions.

osb-18.name: OSB 23/32 in (nominal 3/4 in, 18.3 mm)
osb-18.note: As osb-12; the usual 23/32 in subfloor panel.

shiplap-19x140.name: Shiplap cladding 1×6 (19 × 140 mm)
shiplap-19x140.note: Thickness and 130 mm face (cover) width from PS 20-20 Table 4 (shiplap, 10 mm lap, nominal 6); overall width 140 from Table 3; stock lengths are the plan's assumption.

_meta.note: Largest support spacing for each OSB panel, by use: 16 in. floor for 15/32 in., 24 in. for 23/32 in., 24 in. roof and wall. Rules of thumb for the T4 checks from search summaries of APA span ratings, not from the table itself. Check the panel's stamped span rating.

nail-framing.name: 16d common nail, 3-1/2 in. × 0.162 in.
nail-framing.note: Count per lb is a published figure for common nails (Admiral Steel 47 for 16d, 101 for 8d; Mitek 48 and 94-126 by coating).

nail-toe.name: 8d common nail, 2-1/2 in. × 0.131 in.
nail-toe.note: Count per lb is a published figure for common nails (Admiral Steel 47 for 16d, 101 for 8d; Mitek 48 and 94-126 by coating).

nail-sheathing.name: 8d ring-shank nail, 2-1/2 in. × 0.113 in., galvanized
nail-sheathing.note: Count per lb computed from steel density (formula in docs/research/timber-structures.md), not read from a catalogue. The IRC sheathing row allows 8d common (0.131 in.) as well.

nail-cladding.name: 8d siding nail, 2-1/2 in., galvanized
nail-cladding.note: Count per lb from one distributor's siding-nail list (Admiral Steel), read from a table whose columns were hard to align.

screw-rafter.name: Structural screw 1/4 × 6 in., fully threaded
screw-rafter.note: In the US a hurricane/rafter tie is the usual answer; a long structural screw is shown so the same rule works in both regions. Pack sizes are an assumption.

screw-corner.name: Structural screw 1/4 × 5 in., partly threaded
screw-corner.use: wall panels to each other at the corners
screw-corner.note: Pack sizes are an assumption, not a supplier's catalogue.

bolt-m12.name: Carriage bolt 1/2 × 8 in., galvanized, with nut and two washers
bolt-m12.use: beam plies to a post (a sandwich beam)
bolt-m12.note: Pack sizes are an assumption, not a supplier's catalogue.

screw-deck.name: Deck screw #10 × 2-1/2 in., stainless, torx
screw-deck.use: deck boards onto joists, 2 per joist crossing
screw-deck.note: Pack sizes are an assumption, not a supplier's catalogue.

screw-connector.name: Connector screw #10 × 1-1/2 in., galvanized (for post bases and caps)
screw-connector.note: Many bought post bases come with their own screws or bolts; pack sizes are an assumption.

stud-plate.note: end nails through the plate into the stud end

plate-plate.note: top plates lapped at a corner: 2 face nails

joist-rim.note: end nails through the rim into the joist end, or blocking

rafter-plate.note: 2 toe nails hold the rafter while it is fixed; 1 structural screw per rafter and plate resists uplift

header-trimmer.note: header or sill to king or jack stud: 4 toe nails

sheet-frame.note: one spacing for the whole sheet: the 6 in. edge spacing; field nails could be 12 in. (the joint carries only the length, not edge or field)

board-frame.note: 2 nails where a board crosses a stud

king-jack.note: built-up stud, face nailed at 24 in. o.c.

jack-header.note: header bears on the jack stud; end nails through the header

plate-lap.note: doubled top plate face nailed at 16 in. o.c.

corner-stud.note: the wall panels are fixed to each other at the corners after they are stood up

blocking-rafter.note: blocking or outrigger end nailed through the rafter

fascia-rafter.note: board face nailed to each rafter end

barge-rafter.note: board face nailed along the rafter

rafter-ridge.note: rafter plumb-cut against the ridge board: 4 toe nails and 3 end nails through the ridge board (unverified, from the IRC rafter-to-ridge row)

tie-rafter.note: tie (ceiling joist) face nailed to the rafter at the heel: 4 nails per joint (unverified: the IRC heel joint connection table R802.5.1(9) was not read)

tie-plate.note: tie (ceiling joist) toe nailed to the top plate: 3 nails per joint (unverified: from the IRC ceiling-joist-to-plate row, not read)

post-base.note: post (or beam) into its post base: 4 screws each side (unverified: a bought base comes with its own fixing schedule, follow it)

beam-post.note: a sandwich beam: one ply to the post. A bolt passes through both plies and the post, so one per ply gives two bolts per post, staggered (unverified)

beam-cap.note: a beam on a post cap: the cap's schedule, 4 screws into the post and 4 into the beam per ply (unverified; the cap is listed as a bought item)

beam-ply.note: plies of a built-up beam screwed together every 400 mm, staggered (unverified)

joist-beam.note: joist bearing on a beam ply: two skew screws (or a joist hanger where the joist butts a beam), per ply (unverified)

deck-board.note: two stainless screws where a deck board crosses a joist

brace-post.note: knee brace foot bolted through the post (M12 x 200 passes a 75-89 mm brace and the post); unverified, a builder's rule of thumb

brace-beam.note: knee brace head screwed up into each beam ply: two structural screws per ply (unverified)

rafter-beam.note: rafter on top of the beam, one skew structural screw into each beam ply it crosses (uplift); a hurricane tie is the upgrade for windy sites (unverified, uplift not checked)

slat-rafter.note: one stainless screw where a slat crosses a rafter (unverified)

brace-rafter.note: cross knee brace head screwed up into the rafter over the post: two structural screws (unverified)

_meta.note: Nail and screw counts per joint follow the IRC 2021 fastening schedule R602.3(1) as read from a distributor's chart and the ICC code-change proposal text (see docs/research/timber-structures.md), adapted to the joints the generator records. They are workbench rules, not a code check. Nails are sold by weight, structural screws only where they are stronger (rafter to plate, wall corners). Review before relying on them.

SPF-No2.name: SPF No. 2
SPF-No2.note: Bending, E and G are read from Table 4A. Density is NOT in the table: 450 kg/m3 (about 12% moisture) is derived from G = 0.42 and flagged unverified. Values are allowable-stress reference values, a different basis from EN 338 characteristic strength: T4 must not mix them.

defaults.note: Spacings, items, spare and kerf are workbench defaults from the plan. Loads are placeholder values to be set per site; roof pitch limits per covering were not read from a manufacturer or code and must be checked.

details.note: Platform framing defaults: corner assembly and a double top plate lapped at the corners.

terrace.note: Terrace defaults are workbench choices. The maximum post and row spacings are caps: the generator also keeps each span under 80% of what the span formulas allow. 'min_post_mm': a post shorter than this is left out and the beams sit on the post bases. 'railing_height_mm': a terrace higher than this is flagged as needing a railing.

summer_kitchen.note: Summer kitchen defaults are workbench choices; its posts, beams, braces, footings, floor and walls take the pergola, terrace and shed defaults. 'height_eaves_mm' is the underside of the lower beam above the ground, 'pitch_deg_mono' the slope of a mono roof (a gable roof takes 'pitch_deg'), 'floor_height_mm' the top of the terrace floor above the ground.

pergola.note: Pergola defaults are workbench choices. 'height_mm' is the underside of the beams above the ground. 'overhang_mm' is how far the rafters reach past the outer face of each beam, 'beam_overhang_mm' how far a beam reaches past its end post's centre line. The maximum post spacing is a cap: the generator also keeps each beam span under 80% of what the span formulas allow. Knee braces: 45 degrees, centreline legs of 'brace_leg_mm' (the common builders' figure of about 2 ft; not read from a standard).

sources.title: American Softwood Lumber Standard, Voluntary Product Standard PS 20-20 (NIST, January 2020), Table 3 (boards, dimension) and Table 4 (worked lumber)
sources.note: Minimum dressed dry sizes in mm: 1x4 = 19 x 89, 2x2 = 38 x 38, 2x3 = 38 x 64, 2x4 = 38 x 89, 2x6 = 38 x 140, 2x8 = 38 x 184, 2x10 = 38 x 235, 4x4 = 89 x 89. Shiplap (10 mm lap) nominal 1x6: 19 thick, 130 mm face width.

sources.title: National Design Specification Supplement, 2018 edition (American Wood Council), Table 4A, Spruce-Pine-Fir 'No. 1/No. 2', 2" & wider
sources.note: A retailer-hosted copy of the AWC supplement. Values: Fb 875, Ft 450, Fv 135, Fc-perp 425, Fc 1,150, E 1,400,000, Emin 510,000 psi, specific gravity G 0.42 (NLGA). The table's grade row is 'No. 1/No. 2'. Converted to MPa at 0.00689476 MPa per psi.

sources.title: Workbench build plan, docs/research/timber-structures.md
sources.note: Region scope (16 in on centre, 4 x 8 ft sheets, 8-16 ft stock lengths), item keys and the packs of 100/200/500 come from the plan. These are workbench decisions, not measured facts.

sources.title: APA span ratings: 24/16 (7/16 in.) roof sheathing on 24 in. supports; 19/32 in. Sturd-I-Floor rated 20 oc (24 in. maximum with clips), as found through search summaries (APA E30, county and city code handouts)
sources.note: Search summaries only; APA's own table was not opened. The floor limit for 15/32 in. (16 in.) is a common rule of thumb not confirmed in a source read.

sources.title: Framing nailing schedule labelled IRC 2021 Table R602.3(1) (distributor chart, Albany County Fasteners); ICC Building Code Action Committee proposal text for the 2012/13 cycle of the same table
sources.note: codes.iccsafe.org returned 403 (not readable here), so the table was read second-hand: a distributor's chart labelled IRC 2021 and ICC's 2012/13 proposal (https://www.iccsafe.org/wp-content/uploads/bcac/IRC-TableR60231.pdf). Rows differ a little between editions; check the adopted edition.

sources.title: Approximate common nails per lb: Admiral Steel nail list (16d 47, 8d 101, 8d siding 189) and Mitek nail table (16d 48)
sources.note: Mitek: https://mitek-us.com/wp-content/uploads/files/product/us/tables/Nails.pdf. Counts vary with coating and maker.

sources.title: Ground screw makers (Krinner and similar): range of Ø76 mm screws, about 800 to 1200 mm long, with post brackets or flat head plates
sources.note: NOT read: the page answered HTTP 429 (too many requests) when the workbench tried it. Sizes and the 2 m post spacing are what such ranges typically offer and are marked unverified; read the maker's table for the screw you buy, with the soil it will stand in.

sources.title: Precast concrete pier (deck) blocks with adjustable post bases, and poured concrete footings: common sizes in builders' guides
sources.note: Not read from a maker's page: sizes (a 300 mm block, a 300 mm diameter pier 800 mm deep, a 400 mm square pad) are typical figures. Frost depth, soil and loads decide the real size: check locally.

sources.title: Decking practice: boards 25-28 mm thick on joists at 400-500 mm, a gap of about 5 mm, two stainless screws at every joist, balcony and terrace live load
sources.note: Not read from a datasheet. The 28 x 145 board and the span limit per thickness are the workbench's usual figures; the 25 x 150 board is sold by the supplier in the price snapshot. Check the board maker's span table.

sources.title: IRC 2021 R301.5: live load on decks 40 psf (1.9 kN/m2); R507 deck framing
sources.note: Not read: the 40 psf deck live load is the figure usually quoted from R301.5; R507 span tables were not used. Marked unverified.

sources.title: Pergola building practice: posts 100-150 mm, doubled beams on the posts, rafters at 400-600 mm with an overhang of about 300 mm, slats on top, 45 degree knee braces with legs of about 600 mm (builders' and timber-frame guides)
sources.note: NOT read from a standard or a single page; these are the figures such guides commonly give and are marked unverified. Knee brace angle 45 degrees and leg length about 2 ft are the usual rule of thumb; check local rules and wind loads.
